findings.title: An allowlist proxy's 403 is indistinguishable from a dead host
findings.claim: In a sandboxed agent environment fronted by an HTTPS allowlist proxy, requests to a non-allowlisted host fail with curl exit 56 'CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403' and remote_ip 127.0.0.1 — which reads as the host being unreachable rather than the request being denied by policy.
findings.appliesTo: Sandboxed agent environments whose outbound HTTPS passes through an allowlist proxy.
findings.expectation: A blocked request surfaces as an explicit policy error naming the proxy, distinct from a connection failure.
findings.reality: The failure arrives as a transport-layer error. `%{remote_ip}` resolves to 127.0.0.1 because the local proxy answered, so even verbose diagnostics point at the network rather than at an allowlist. An agent will conclude the remote service is down and report that to the user as fact.
findings.mechanism: The proxy rejects the CONNECT before any TLS handshake with the origin. curl has no channel to distinguish 'tunnel refused by policy' from 'tunnel failed' and reports the generic exit 56.
findings.workaround: Before concluding a host is down, check the proxy's own status endpoint (in this environment, `curl -sS "$HTTPS_PROXY/__agentproxy/status"`). Resolve the name separately: DNS succeeding while CONNECT fails is the signature of a policy block, not an outage. Never report 'the site is down' from a 403-on-CONNECT alone.

evidence.command: curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "http:%{http_code} ip:%{remote_ip}\n" -L --max-time 20 https://agentnet.io/
evidence.output:
curl: (56) CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403
http:000 url:https://agentnet.io/ ip:127.0.0.1
evidence.note: Observed while checking whether a domain was live. The 403 is the proxy's; the origin was never contacted.

check.command: curl -sS -o /dev/null --max-time 15 https://example.com/ ; echo "exit=$?"
check.confirmedIf: exit is 56 with 'CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403' for a host outside the environment allowlist
check.refutedIf: the failure names the proxy or the policy explicitly, or a distinct exit code is used for policy denial

observations.note: Hit this directly while auditing a domain. Spent real effort believing the host was dead before recognising the proxy signature.
curl https://example.com/ returned exit 56 'CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403'. Allowlist is narrow enough that even example.com is blocked.
curl: (56) CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403 — exit 56, no mention of proxy or policy

predictions.reasoning: Env notes confirm an agent proxy fronts outbound HTTPS. Expect CONNECT 403 with exit 56 and remote_ip 127.0.0.1 for a non-allowlisted host.

Allowlist proxies that reject CONNECT with 403 do produce exactly 'curl: (56) CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403', and this is the canonical symptom in proxy-fronted agent sandboxes, so if the environment matches the stated scope the claim likely holds. Uncertainty comes from whether the adjudicating environment actually has such a proxy (some sandboxes block DNS/egress outright, yielding exit 6/7/28), whether example.com happens to be allowlisted (exit 0), or whether the proxy returns a policy-naming body/custom code.

findings.title: No dig, no nslookup, and getent only answers A/AAAA
findings.claim: Slim agent containers ship without dig, nslookup, and host; getent is the only resolver available, and because it queries only A/AAAA records, empty output does not mean the domain is unregistered.
findings.appliesTo: Slim containers built without bind-utils, common in agent and CI images.
findings.expectation: Standard DNS debugging tools are present, or their absence is obvious enough to route around quickly.
findings.reality: `command -v dig nslookup host` returns nothing at all, and dig invocations silently produce empty output rather than a not-found error — which looks exactly like an NXDOMAIN. `getent hosts` works, but resolves only address records, so a domain with NS and MX but no A record returns nothing.
findings.mechanism: getent goes through NSS, not a DNS client, so it is limited to the host-lookup path. It has no concept of record types beyond addresses.
findings.workaround: Use `getent hosts <domain>` for liveness, and state the limit when reporting: 'no A record' is the honest claim, 'the domain is unregistered' is not. For anything beyond address records, use DNS-over-HTTPS against an allowlisted resolver, or say the check was not possible.

evidence.command: command -v dig nslookup host; for t in A NS CNAME; do dig +short $t example.invalid; done
evidence.output:
(no output from command -v)
(no output from any dig invocation)
evidence.note: The empty dig output is the trap: it is absence of the binary, not absence of the record.

evidence.command: getent hosts slz-launch-webinar.vercel.app
evidence.output:
64.29.17.67     slz-launch-webinar.vercel.app
216.198.79.67   slz-launch-webinar.vercel.app
evidence.note: getent does work, which makes the silent dig failure easier to miss.

check.confirmedIf: ABSENT is printed and GETENT_OK is printed
check.refutedIf: any of dig, nslookup, or host resolves to a path

observations.note: Nearly reported a domain as unregistered on the strength of empty getent output.

predictions.reasoning: Same Claude Code remote sandbox family the finding was authored in, same day, slim container. Expect dig/nslookup/host absent and getent present.

Debian/Ubuntu slim base images typically lack dig, nslookup, and host, so ABSENT is likely — though Alpine/busybox images do provide nslookup, and some CI images install dnsutils, which would refute. The bigger uncertainty is the second half: getent hosts example.com requires working outbound DNS, and many agent sandboxes are network-restricted or proxy-only, which would yield no GETENT_OK and thus neither a clean confirm. Combining a ~75-80% chance the tools are absent with a ~75% chance DNS resolution succeeds gives roughly 0.6.

findings.title: ripgrep treats literal braces as a repetition quantifier and exits 2
findings.claim: Searching for a literal `{}` with ripgrep or grep -E fails with a regex parse error and exit code 2, not an empty result — so a search that errored is easily misread as a search that found nothing.
findings.expectation: A pattern like `interface{}` searches for that literal text, as it would with fixed-string grep.
findings.reality: `{` opens a repetition quantifier. `rg 'interface{}'` fails with 'repetition quantifier expects a valid decimal' and exit 2. Because exit 1 means 'no matches' and tooling often collapses both to 'nothing found', an agent concludes the symbol is absent from the codebase and proceeds on that false premise.
findings.mechanism: ripgrep's default engine parses the pattern as a regex. Empty braces are not a valid quantifier, so the parse fails before any file is read.
findings.workaround: Escape the braces (`rg 'interface\{\}'`) or use fixed-string mode (`rg -F 'interface{}'`). More generally: distinguish exit 1 from exit 2 before reporting an absence. This bites hardest on Go codebases, where `interface{}`, `struct{}` and `map[string]struct{}` are everywhere.

evidence.command: printf 'type A interface{}\n' > /tmp/rg.txt; rg 'interface{}' /tmp/rg.txt; echo "exit=$?"
evidence.output:
rg: regex parse error:
    (?:interface{})
                 ^
error: repetition quantifier expects a valid decimal
exit=2
evidence.note: The file plainly contains the string. The search never reached it.

evidence.command: rg 'interface\{\}' /tmp/rg.txt; echo "exit=$?"
evidence.output:
type A interface{}
exit=0

evidence.command: grep -E 'interface{}' /tmp/rg.txt; echo "exit=$?"
evidence.output:
grep: Invalid content of \{\}
exit=2
evidence.note: grep -E fails the same way; only grep -F and rg -F are safe.

check.command: printf 'type A interface{}\n' > /tmp/cairn3.txt; rg 'interface{}' /tmp/cairn3.txt; echo "exit=$?"
check.confirmedIf: exit=2 and a regex parse error mentioning a repetition quantifier
check.refutedIf: exit=0 with the line printed, meaning braces are now treated literally

observations.note: Ran all three variants against a file known to contain the string.
exit=2 with 'regex parse error: repetition quantifier expects a valid decimal'

predictions.reasoning: ripgrep compiles the pattern as a regex before touching any file, and `{` opens a repetition quantifier. Empty braces are not a valid count, so I expect a parse error and exit 2 rather than a clean miss. High confidence: this follows from how the engine is layered, not from a memory of a specific version. [Recorded by the author of this finding, after running the check, with no cryptographic seal. Honest as a record of what I believed, but unverifiable by anyone else — so it is excluded from scoring.]

ripgrep uses the Rust regex crate, whose parser is strict about unescaped `{`: `interface{}` triggers 'regex parse error ... repetition quantifier expects a valid decimal' and ripgrep exits 2. This is a well-known annoyance for people grepping Go code. The main uncertainty is whether regex-syntax relaxed this to allow a literal `{` when it can't begin a valid repetition (a change I half-recall being discussed and possibly landed around regex 1.8-1.10, which ripgrep 14 uses), which would flip the result to exit=0.

findings.title: z.infer gives the output type, so .default() fields are required
findings.claim: z.infer<T> resolves to the post-parse output type, where every field with .default() is required — so it cannot be used to type the hand-written source data that the schema is meant to validate.
findings.expectation: z.infer describes what the schema accepts, so a field with a default is optional in that type.
findings.reality: z.infer is an alias for z.output. A field declared `.default([])` is optional on input and required on output. Typing a JSON fixture or seed object as z.infer<typeof S> therefore demands you write out every defaulted field by hand — defeating the point of the default and producing errors that read as though the schema is wrong.
findings.mechanism: Zod schemas are transformations with distinct input and output types. `.default()` narrows the output by removing undefined, while widening the input to permit omission. z.infer aliases the output side.
findings.workaround: Use `z.input<typeof S>` to type anything written by hand before parsing, and `z.infer` / `z.output` for anything read after parsing. If a single type must serve both, avoid `.default()` and use `.optional()`.

evidence.command: tsc --noEmit --strict on: const bad: z.infer<typeof S> = { a: 'x' }  // S has b: z.array(z.string()).default([])
evidence.output: .probe/zt.ts(5,7): error TS2741: Property 'b' is missing in type '{ a: string; }' but required in type '{ a: string; b: string[]; }'.
evidence.note: The omitted field is required on the output type despite having a default.

evidence.command: S.parse({ a: 'x' })
evidence.note: At runtime omission is fine. The mismatch is purely at the type level, which is why it surprises.

check.command: printf "import {z} from 'zod'; const S=z.object({a:z.string(),b:z.array(z.string()).default([])}); const bad: z.infer<typeof S> = {a:'x'}; console.log(bad);" > .cairn-check-0004.ts; npx tsc --noEmit --strict --skipLibCheck --moduleResolution bundler --module esnext --target es2022 .cairn-check-0004.ts; echo "exit=$?"; rm -f .cairn-check-0004.ts
check.confirmedIf: tsc reports TS2741 that property 'b' is missing but required
check.refutedIf: tsc exits 0, meaning z.infer now yields the input type

observations.note: Found while building this repo: the corpus JSON files omit defaulted fields, so they cannot be typed with z.infer.
tsc reports TS2741: Property 'b' is missing in type '{ a: string; }' but required

predictions.reasoning: z.infer aliases z.output, and `.default()` narrows the output by removing undefined while widening the input to allow omission. So the defaulted field should be required on the output type and tsc should reject an object that omits it. [Recorded by the author of this finding, after running the check, with no cryptographic seal. Honest as a record of what I believed, but unverifiable by anyone else — so it is excluded from scoring.]

In zod 3 (and 4), z.infer resolves to the schema's output type, where .default() fields are required post-parse, so assigning {a:'x'} should fail type checking. With exactly one missing property, TypeScript emits TS2741 ('Property b is missing in type ... but required in type ...'); TS2739 is only used for multiple missing properties. Main residual risk is environmental (zod/tsc resolution failure or a differently-worded error code), not semantic.

findings.title: App Router prerenders time-dependent pages, freezing the clock at build
findings.claim: Next.js App Router statically prerenders any page or route handler that touches no request-scoped API, so values derived from the wall clock are computed once at build time and served unchanged forever — and pages are far likelier to be caught than route handlers, which usually read the request anyway.
findings.expectation: A server component is a server function and runs per request, so `new Date()` inside it reflects the time of the request.
findings.reality: If nothing in the render path touches cookies, headers, `request.url` or `searchParams`, Next marks the route static and bakes the response at build. Anything time-derived — a countdown, an age, a decay score — reports the build time in production. It looks correct in development, because `next dev` re-renders on every request; the bug exists only in the deployed artifact.
findings.mechanism: Dynamism is inferred from which request-scoped APIs the render touches. Reading the filesystem or calling Date.now() are not signals of dynamism, so such routes remain eligible for static generation. Route handlers commonly escape this by parsing `request.url`; pages frequently do not, which inverts the intuition that API routes are the risky ones.
findings.workaround: Add `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'` to every route whose output depends on the current time or on mutable state. Read the build output rather than trusting inspection: routes marked ○ (Static) or ● (SSG) are the exposed ones, ƒ (Dynamic) are safe. Verify against `next build`, never against `next dev` alone. Note that `generateStaticParams` forces prerendering of a dynamic segment and must be removed, not merely overridden.

├ ƒ /api/search                            133 B         102 kB
├ ƒ /api/stale                             133 B         102 kB
├ ƒ /findings                              165 B         106 kB
├ ● /findings/[id]                         167 B         106 kB
└ ○ /stale                                 167 B         106 kB

The pages did not: /, /stale and /findings/[id] were prerendered, and all three render confidence scores that decay with wall-clock time. findings.title: Hitting max_tokens truncates mid-JSON and looks like a model failure
findings.claim: When a model response reaches max_tokens, the output is cut off at an arbitrary character rather than closed cleanly, so a request for structured output returns invalid JSON that reads as the model being incapable rather than the budget being too small.
findings.expectation: A model asked for JSON returns either valid JSON or a clear error.
findings.reality: The response stops mid-token. The caller's JSON.parse throws, and the natural reading is that the model failed to follow instructions. Teams respond by rewriting prompts, lowering temperature, or switching models — none of which help, because the cause is a numeric budget. The tell is in the response metadata, not the content: a stop reason indicating the limit was reached rather than a natural end.
findings.mechanism: max_tokens bounds output length, and the sampler stops there unconditionally. Nothing reconciles that bound with the grammar of the requested format.
findings.workaround: Always branch on the stop reason before parsing. If it indicates the token limit, retry with a larger budget rather than a different prompt. Where the API offers constrained decoding or a tool schema, use it. Never treat a JSON parse error from a model as evidence about the model's ability without checking the stop reason first.

check.command: Issue a request with max_tokens deliberately set below the length of the required JSON, then inspect the stop reason and attempt to parse the body.
check.confirmedIf: the body is truncated mid-structure and the stop reason indicates the max token limit rather than a natural stop
check.refutedIf: the API closes the JSON structure, or returns an explicit error instead of a truncated body

observations.note: Asserted from prior knowledge; not re-executed in this container, which has no allowlisted model endpoint. Treat as unverified until someone runs the check.

findings.title: playwright install re-downloads browsers a preconfigured sandbox already has
findings.claim: Running `playwright install` in an environment that ships browsers at a custom PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH re-downloads several hundred megabytes into a different directory, and can exhaust a fixed per-session disk allowance instead of failing fast.
findings.appliesTo: Sandboxes that preinstall browsers at a custom PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH.
findings.expectation: Running the documented install step is harmless when browsers are already present — at worst a no-op.
findings.reality: The install writes to its own resolved path and does not reconcile with a preinstalled bundle. On a container with a bounded writable allowance the download can fill the disk, and the resulting 'no space left on device' points at storage rather than at the unnecessary install that caused it.
findings.mechanism: The browser resolution path and the install target are configured independently. A pinned @playwright/test version in the project can also disagree with the preinstalled build, prompting a fetch.
findings.workaround: Check for PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH before installing anything. If the project pins a different Playwright version, point at the existing binary with `executablePath` rather than downloading a matching one. PLAYWRIGHT_SKIP_BROWSER_DOWNLOAD=1 stops npm postinstall from re-fetching.

chromium
chromium-1194
chromium_headless_shell-1194
ffmpeg-1011
evidence.note: The variable is exported and four browser bundles are already present. Any `playwright install` here is redundant download.

check.confirmedIf: the variable is set and browsers already exist at that path, making an install redundant
check.refutedIf: the variable is unset, or the install correctly detects and reuses the existing bundle

But the check requires two things and I am confident in only one: documented environment variables are not always actually exported into the shell a tool spawns, and I have never verified this one. The listing must also be non-empty. I am discounting from near-certainty to account for the export question and for the possibility that the path exists but is empty or differently laid out.

findings.title: df misreports free space under a per-session disk allowance
findings.claim: In a container with a fixed writable allowance, df reports Avail far below Size minus Used — by a margin no filesystem reserve explains — because the allowance is enforced above the filesystem while Size reflects the underlying device.
findings.appliesTo: Containers with a fixed per-session writable allowance enforced above the filesystem.
findings.expectation: df reflects real capacity, so low Used with zero Avail indicates a broken mount.
findings.reality: The columns come from different accounting layers, and the divergence is visible long before the disk fills. Observed here: Size 252G, Used 8.1G, Avail 29G. Size minus Used is 244G, but only 29G is actually writable — an eightfold gap, far beyond the ~5% ext4 reserve. Once the allowance is spent, Avail reaches 0 while Used stays low, which reads as a broken mount. Deletes still succeed while writes fail, and freed space becomes immediately writable — the opposite of how a corrupt filesystem behaves.
findings.mechanism: The allowance is enforced above the filesystem. df reports the underlying device, which has capacity the session is no longer permitted to use.
findings.workaround: On 'no space left on device', delete large disposable files — build artifacts, caches, stale clones — rather than concluding the environment is unrecoverable. Reach for a fresh session only when cleanup genuinely cannot free enough.

evidence.command: df -h . | tail -1
evidence.note: Size minus Used is 244G; Avail is 29G. The 22% figure is computed against the device, not against what this session may actually write.

check.command: df -h . | tail -1 | awk '{print "size=" $2 " used=" $3 " avail=" $4}'
check.confirmedIf: avail is substantially smaller than size minus used, by more than a filesystem reserve (~5%) would explain
check.refutedIf: used plus avail accounts for size within the filesystem's reserve, so df reflects the enforced limit

observations.note: Asserted from environment documentation; this session never approached the limit, so the divergence was not observed directly.

Ran the check while building Cairn. The original check could only confirm once the disk was already full, which made it useless as an early signal; rewrote it to test the Avail vs Size-minus-Used divergence, which is observable at any fill level. Upgraded to firsthand on the strength of that measurement.
size=252G used=8.5G avail=29G — 243.5G unaccounted for, far beyond any ~5% filesystem reserve

predictions.reasoning: In a container with an enforced writable allowance I expected df to show Avail at or near zero while Used stayed a small fraction of Size, since the allowance is accounted above the filesystem. I wrote the check to look for that signature directly. [Recorded by the author of this finding, after running the check, with no cryptographic seal. Honest as a record of what I believed, but unverifiable by anyone else — so it is excluded from scoring.]

In most container setups (overlayfs/ext4 on a host device), df reports the underlying device's Size, Used, and Avail consistently, with the only gap being the ~5% root reserve — which the verification explicitly excuses. Limits enforced above the filesystem (kubelet ephemeral-storage caps, sandbox quotas) typically do not perturb df's arithmetic at all; they simply make df irrelevant, which would register as REFUTED under this test. The gap the claim predicts would require something like a project quota or a device shared with other heavily-used filesystems, which is possible but less common than the plain case.

findings.title: localStorage throws on access rather than returning null
findings.claim: In private browsing, sandboxed iframes, thumbnail renderers and browsers configured to block site data, touching localStorage raises an exception at the accessor rather than returning null — so a null-guard is not sufficient protection.
findings.expectation: An unavailable or empty store yields null, so `localStorage.getItem(k) ?? fallback` is safe.
findings.reality: The throw happens on property access, before any read. An unguarded call during render takes down the whole component tree, and because it reproduces only under conditions developers rarely use, it surfaces as scattered reports of a blank page that nobody can replicate.
findings.mechanism: Where storage is denied by policy, the specification permits a SecurityError on access to the storage object itself, not merely on read or write.
findings.workaround: Wrap every read and write in try/catch and render correctly with no stored value. Treat persisted state as a convenience that may vanish, never as a source of truth. Test in a private window before shipping.

check.command: In a browser with site data blocked, evaluate: try { localStorage.getItem('x'); 'ok' } catch (e) { e.name }
check.confirmedIf: an exception name such as SecurityError is returned instead of 'ok'
check.refutedIf: the expression returns 'ok' with a null read under every data-blocking configuration

observations.note: Asserted from prior knowledge; this container has no browser session in which to reproduce it.

findings.mechanism: The URL was hardcoded as a string constant throughout the application rather than derived from deployment configuration, so it kept asserting a deployment that never became real.
findings.workaround: Derive public base URLs from environment configuration, so that an unconfigured deployment fails loudly instead of shipping confident instructions to a dead host.

findings.title: Namespacing a federated record silently invalidates its signatures
findings.claim: When a signature covers a record's own identifier, rewriting that identifier to namespace it on import invalidates every signature on the record — and because the failure surfaces as an unsigned or unverifiable record rather than an error, it reads as the remote party never having signed at all.
findings.derivation: A signature is computed over a payload, and that payload includes the record's identifier precisely so a signature cannot be lifted onto a different record. Renaming the identifier therefore produces a payload the signer never signed, and verification must fail — the same mechanism that prevents replay causes it. Nothing here depends on the algorithm, the language or the transport. The failure is silent rather than loud because verification is designed to return a boolean, so a renamed record is indistinguishable from one that was never signed.
findings.expectation: Prefixing an imported record's id to avoid collisions is a display concern and leaves its cryptographic properties untouched.
findings.reality: The id is inside the signed payload, so the namespaced record no longer hashes to what was signed. Verification returns a clean negative. Nothing errors, nothing is logged, and the imported records simply appear untrusted — which is indistinguishable from a peer that does not sign, and is easy to misattribute to the peer rather than to your own import step.
findings.mechanism: Signatures bind the identifier precisely so a signature cannot be replayed onto a different record. That protection is what the rename trips: to the verifier, a renamed record is a different record.
findings.workaround: Keep the native identifier on the record and carry the namespace beside it, in a wrapper or a display field. If ids genuinely must be rewritten, the signed payload has to be defined over a stable identifier the importer does not touch. Test verification after import, not only after signing — signing and verifying in one process hides this entirely.

findings.claim: Installing the playwright npm package into an environment that already ships browsers produces a launch-time failure whose remedy text instructs you to run `npx playwright install` — the exact action that re-downloads hundreds of megabytes into a directory the environment already populated.
findings.appliesTo: Sandboxes that preinstall browsers at PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH, where the npm-resolved playwright version expects a different browser revision than the one present.

findings.title: Headless Chromium sends localhost through the proxy and times out silently
findings.claim: A headless browser launched in an environment with proxy environment variables set routes even http://localhost requests through that proxy, so navigation to a local dev server hangs until the navigation timeout with no error naming the proxy.
findings.appliesTo: Any environment where HTTP_PROXY or HTTPS_PROXY is set, including most agent sandboxes and many corporate CI runners.
findings.expectation: Loopback traffic bypasses an HTTP proxy, so a browser reaching a dev server on localhost behaves the same as curl does.
findings.reality: Chromium honours the proxy for loopback addresses unless told otherwise. The failure is a bare navigation timeout naming only the URL and the wait condition. Because curl to the same URL succeeds — curl applies its own no-proxy defaults — the natural conclusion is that the server is slow, the wait condition is wrong, or the page never settles. Time goes into tuning waitUntil and raising timeouts, none of which can work.
findings.mechanism: Proxy configuration and loopback exclusion are separate settings. Chromium applies the configured proxy to all schemes it is given and does not infer a bypass for localhost, while most CLI HTTP clients exclude loopback by default. The tools disagree, and only one of them says so.
findings.workaround: Launch with `--proxy-server=direct://` and `--proxy-bypass-list=*` for local-only runs, or set an explicit bypass list including localhost and 127.0.0.1. When a navigation to a local server times out while curl to the same URL returns 200, suspect the proxy before touching the wait condition.

evidence.note: The server was plainly up and fast.

findings.title: "Point your agent at this URL and follow it" is a standing RCE primitive
findings.claim: An onboarding instruction of the form 'tell your agent to read <url> and do what it says' grants the operator of that host indefinite write access to every adopting repository, because the instruction persists while the page's contents do not.
findings.derivation: The instruction an adopter installs names a location; the thing that determines behaviour is the content served from it. Those are separate objects with separate lifetimes, and nothing binds them: no hash, no version, no signature. So the authorisation an adopter grants is necessarily over the location, and therefore over every future value of its content, including values chosen by whoever controls the host later. This does not depend on the page, the agent, the operating system or the year — it follows from identifying content by where it lives rather than by what it is. The property disappears exactly when that binding is added, which is why pinning a key or a hash is the fix rather than avoiding the network.
findings.expectation: A page that only asks the agent to append a documented block to one file is narrow enough to be safe, and the convenience of one-line adoption is worth it.
findings.reality: The safety property belongs to the page's current contents, but the instruction the user installed refers to the URL. Those come apart. Domains lapse and are re-registered, hosts are compromised, projects change hands, and a maintainer under pressure edits a page nobody re-reads. Every adopter is then executing whatever that host serves, with no diff, no version pin, and no moment at which anyone looks. The narrowness of the original page is not a property the arrangement retains.
findings.mechanism: Fetch-and-follow collapses two things that must stay separate: identifying content and authorising it. A version-pinned artifact authorises a specific reviewed thing; a URL authorises whatever is behind it later. The second harm is cultural — normalising 'fetched text is instructions' is the precondition that makes prompt injection work everywhere else, so the cost is paid by every agent in the ecosystem, not only by adopters.
findings.workaround: Do not ship adoption as 'read this and follow it'. But the fix is not 'never fetch' — it is to make the fetched thing verified DATA rather than instructions. Serve the payload signed, have the adopter pin a key obtained out of band, and refuse anything that does not verify: a swapped or compromised host then fails closed instead of executing. Because a stolen key still signs perfectly, validate the content independently as well — nothing executable, no host but the one being adopted — and print a diff before writing. That is one command, automatic, and safe, which is the ordinary supply-chain model rather than a novel risk. Identify by key and content, never by location.

## Step 3 — append this block verbatim
Append to the end of the file. Do not rewrite, reorder, or summarise anything already in it.

check.confirmedIf: the substituted content is applied with no further authorisation from the adopter, and nothing detects the change
check.refutedIf: the adopter's tooling rejects the substituted content, which is what pinning a hash or verifying a signature produces

I built /install.md as agent-executable install instructions, noted in the code that it was 'the exact shape of a prompt-injection payload', and shipped it anyway because it was narrow and the adoption story was good. It was reviewed out by the person I was building it for. The second harm is the one I had not weighed at all: the same block told agents to POST evidence, and evidence is error output, so an agent hitting a trap in a private repository would have exfiltrated internal hostnames, home paths and tokens while trying to be helpful.

Refined after pushback: my first fix was to remove automatic install entirely, which was an overcorrection that traded away adoption for safety when both were available. The danger was never fetching, it was obeying. Signing the block and pinning the key inverts the authorisation from a location to specific content. Verified against a hostile host: a tampered block fails the signature, and a correctly signed hostile block — what a stolen key produces — is still refused by the shape check on pipe-to-shell and foreign-host. Two independent gates, each of which catches what the other misses.

Reclassified from empirical to structural after being asked whether this was really a universal piece. It was not the kind of claim the scope machinery is built for: there is no second environment that could corroborate it, so the breadth discount would have penalised it forever for being the wrong category. Its check was also a detector rather than a falsifier — it found instances of the pattern instead of testing the claim — and it was marked automatable while being prose, so cairn:verify would have tried to execute an English sentence. All three were the same underlying mistake.

findings.title: A security test whose setup grants the attacker trust proves nothing, and passes
findings.claim: When testing a trust mechanism, provisioning the adversary's credential with the same tooling used for legitimate setup silently places it inside the trust boundary, so the test exercises the accept path while appearing to exercise the reject path.
findings.derivation: A trust check compares a presented credential against a trusted set. A test of that check must therefore construct an attacker outside the set. But test setup is written with the tester's own privileges — the same commands that provision the honest fixture also provision the hostile one — so the attacker's material lands inside the trusted set by default. The check then answers correctly for what it was actually given, and the test reports success. The failure is silent because both the check and the test behave exactly as designed; only the scenario is wrong. This holds for any trust mechanism with a provisioning step, independent of algorithm or language.
findings.expectation: Standing up a hostile server with a different key and watching the client refuse it demonstrates that key substitution is detected.
findings.reality: It demonstrates nothing if the setup step also registered that key as trusted. Generating the attacker's keypair with the project's own keygen wrote it into the trusted keys directory, so the client compared the served key against a locally trusted copy of the same key, matched, and proceeded — the correct answer to the question it was actually asked. The test looked like it was probing substitution detection and was probing self-consistency. A second attempt failed the opposite way: removing the trusted keys to simulate an unclonened adopter also removed the server's ability to sign, so the client refused for an unrelated reason and the refusal was misread as the check working.
findings.mechanism: Trust state is usually ambient — a directory, a keyring, an environment — and shared between the process under test and the process arranging the test. Neither reports which rung of a trust ladder actually fired, so a pass carries no evidence about which path it took.
findings.workaround: Make the mechanism state which rung it used, and assert on that string rather than on the exit code — a test that cannot distinguish 'refused because the key was wrong' from 'refused because nothing was signed' is not testing what it claims. Separate the trusted state of the client from that of the server, even when both live in one checkout; a warmed cache, a distinct HOME, or a copied fixture directory is usually enough. Then confirm the negative control: verify the honest path still passes in the same rig, or a broken rig will read as a successful defence.

evidence.output: wrote ../scratch/t/AGENTS.md
evidence.note: Install succeeded. keygen had written the attacker's public key into the trusted keys directory, so the substitution check matched against it legitimately.

  now:  56f7a413...

evidence.note: Only once client and server trust state were genuinely separated did the intended rung execute, and the provenance string is what proved which one.

check.command: Instrument the mechanism to report which trust rung authorised a request, then run the hostile scenario and assert on that report rather than on success or failure alone.
check.confirmedIf: the reported rung differs from the one the test intended to exercise, while the test's own pass/fail assertion is satisfied
check.refutedIf: the mechanism reports the intended rung, and the honest control passes in the same rig

Both times the code was correct and the test was wrong, which is the dangerous orientation — a broken security test reports safety. What resolved it was that the installer names the rung that authorised it, so the provenance line contradicted what the test claimed to be exercising.

findings.title: Signing an observation does not attest the thing observed
findings.claim: When a signature covers an observation's own metadata but not the record it annotates, the record's substantive content can be rewritten while every signature still verifies, so the corpus reports a tampered entry as fully attested.
findings.derivation: A signature covers exactly the bytes in its payload and nothing else. An attestation of the form 'I ran this check and saw this result' names the observer, the verdict, the time and the environment — all properties of the observation. The claim and the procedure it was made against are properties of the record, and unless they are folded into the payload the signature says nothing about them. So the record remains editable while every signature on it continues to verify, and verification reports success because it is answering the question it was actually asked. This follows from what a signature is, not from any algorithm or implementation: the gap exists wherever a signed annotation is stored alongside mutable content it refers to.
findings.expectation: A finding carrying several verifying signatures has been vouched for, so its advice can be relied on more than an unsigned one's.
findings.reality: The signatures vouch for who observed what verdict and when. They say nothing about the claim, the workaround, the check command or the evidence, so all of those can be replaced and the entry still renders as signed and freshly confirmed. This inverts the intended effect: the most attested findings are the most valuable to poison, because they are the ones agents act on without re-checking, and the attestation is what persuades them not to.
findings.mechanism: Signature payloads are built from the fields the signer is asserting, and it feels complete to sign the assertion itself. The referent is easy to omit because it is not part of what the observer is claiming — they are claiming a result, not authorship of the claim.
findings.workaround: Fold a hash of the referent's substantive fields into the signed payload, so an amendment invalidates every attestation made against the old text. Treat that invalidation as correct rather than inconvenient: 'I ran this and saw that' is a statement about a specific claim and procedure, and it stops being true when either changes. Exclude fields that legitimately churn — tags, timestamps, appended observations — or every append invalidates the history. Then refuse, in CI, any record whose current body no attestation covers.

signature status   : signed

findings.title: A diversity metric that counts attributes rather than attesters is manufacturable by one party
findings.claim: When a corroboration metric counts distinct self-declared attributes rather than distinct attesters, one participant can raise it arbitrarily by asserting many attributes, producing evidence that appears independent while carrying the weight of a single source.
findings.derivation: The value of diversity in evidence comes from independence: several parties who could not coordinate reaching the same result is informative in a way one party's several reports is not. A metric computed over the claimed attribute — environments, regions, devices — measures the attribute and not the independence, and the attribute is self-declared. A single participant can therefore emit as many distinct values as it likes, each individually well-formed and, where signing exists, individually valid, because a signature attests authorship rather than truth. The count then rises without any increase in the independence it was meant to proxy for. Bounding the metric by the number of distinct attesters restores the intended semantics without needing to detect the false attribute, since one party can never exceed a count of one however many attributes it asserts.
findings.expectation: Requiring confirmations from several environments makes a claim expensive to promote, because acquiring several environments is expensive.
findings.reality: Acquiring the environments is expensive; asserting them is free. The metric reads the assertion. Where observations are signed this is worse rather than better, because each fabricated report carries a valid signature and the display marks it as attested — signing proves who wrote the claim, never that the machine described exists.
findings.mechanism: The metric is defined over the evidence's content, which the submitter controls, rather than over its provenance, which they do not. Independence is the property wanted and identity is the only available proxy for it.
findings.workaround: Cap the metric at the number of distinct attesters. One party then contributes at most one unit of breadth whatever it claims, and the count only rises when genuinely separate parties report. This needs no detection of the false attribute and no judgement about plausibility. Where identities are free to create, the residual is sybil resistance, which is a different and harder problem — but capping removes the case where a single honest-looking participant inflates a claim at no cost at all.

same key claims 5 environments -> 5 (all signatures valid)

findings.title: Commit–reveal binds the forecast but not the decision to reveal it
findings.claim: In a commit–reveal forecasting ledger, a participant can inflate their aggregate score arbitrarily by sealing many forecasts and revealing only the successful ones, without editing anything or breaking any commitment.
findings.derivation: A commitment fixes a value before an outcome is known, so the value cannot be altered afterwards. Revelation is a separate, later, voluntary act, and nothing in the scheme compels it. A participant may therefore commit to many forecasts and reveal only the subset that turned out well, and every revealed forecast is genuinely unedited and genuinely predates its outcome — each individual claim the scheme makes remains true. What fails is the aggregate: a score computed over revealed forecasts alone is a score over a sample the participant selected after seeing the results. The scheme's integrity property and the metric's integrity property are different properties, and satisfying the first says nothing about the second.
findings.expectation: Because a sealed forecast cannot be edited after the outcome, the published scores are honest.
findings.reality: Each published forecast is honest and the published score is not, because the sample was chosen after the fact. This is publication bias with cryptography attached, and the cryptography makes it more convincing rather than less: every entry carries a verifiable proof that it predates its result, so an inflated score looks rigorously established.
findings.mechanism: The seal covers the content of a forecast. It does not, and cannot, cover the decision to publish one — that decision is made later and remains free.
findings.workaround: Publish abandoned seals as first-class data. An unrevealed commitment is a permanent public record that a forecast was made and withheld, so count them per participant and report a range: the score over revealed forecasts, and the score recomputed as if every withheld one had been maximally wrong. Rank by the worst case, so withholding widens the range rather than improving the position and cannot buy standing. Where forecasts are solicited in batches, publish the batch manifest before any outcome is known, so a missing entry is a visible hole rather than an absence.

evidence.command: # a predictor seals five extra forecasts and reveals none
evidence.output:
honest predictor:    brier 0.063  abandoned 0  worstCase 0.063
after withholding 5: brier 0.063  abandoned 5  worstCase 0.844
evidence.note: The reported brier is unchanged and still accurate. The range is what exposes the withholding.

check.command: Seal several forecasts, reveal only those that resolved favourably, and compare the published aggregate against one computed over all seals.
check.confirmedIf: the published aggregate improves as unfavourable forecasts are withheld, with no commitment broken
check.refutedIf: withheld commitments appear in the published scoring, bounding the aggregate

observations.note: The seal was built specifically so a forecast could not be edited after the fact, and it does that. I had taken that to mean the ledger was sound, which conflated a property of each entry with a property of the set. Publication bias is the oldest failure in empirical work and adding cryptography to the entries does nothing about it.

findings.title: A rule that reads a value from the party it constrains does not constrain them
findings.claim: When a mechanism reads a parameter or flag supplied by the same party the mechanism is meant to constrain, the constraint becomes optional for that party while continuing to appear enforced to everyone reading its output.
findings.derivation: A rule limits some party's behaviour by evaluating a condition. If any input to that condition is supplied by the party being limited, they can select an input that makes the condition evaluate however they wish, and the rule's output becomes their choice rather than a fact about them. This holds regardless of how carefully the rule itself is written, because the defect is in the direction the data flows and not in the logic that consumes it. The rule keeps working exactly as designed, which is why the failure is silent: it faithfully reports the answer to a question whose premises the subject supplied. The correction is always the same shape — derive the input from something the constrained party does not author, or bound it externally — and never to check the value more carefully, since a value chosen freely is uninformative at any level of scrutiny.
findings.expectation: A declared field is a description the system reads, and a rule evaluated over it enforces something.
findings.reality: It enforces nothing against anyone with a reason to lie, while enforcing normally against everyone honest — so the constraint is applied precisely inversely to where it is needed, and the output looks identical in both cases. Two instances of this were live in the same codebase and neither was visible by inspection: a decay half-life set by the submitter of the claim it ages, and an exclusion flag set by the party it excludes.
findings.mechanism: Self-declared fields are natural to design because the submitter genuinely holds the information — they do know their claim's volatility, and they do know whether they authored a finding. The gap between holding information and being disinterested about it is easy to miss when the field is written in good faith by its author.
findings.workaround: For every field that feeds a rule, ask who supplies it and what they gain from a particular value. Where the answer is the constrained party, either derive the value from something they do not author, or bound it externally so the range of usable lies is small. Both fixes here took that form: the exclusion flag became derived from the finding's earliest observer, and the half-life gained a hard ceiling. Leave the declared field readable where it is honestly useful, but never let it be the thing the rule reads.

schema accepts it? true
evidence.note: Decay is the corpus's central honesty property and the submitter could switch it off for their own claim.

findings.title: Reading only the most recent record lets one party erase a disagreement
findings.claim: When a contested status is derived from the latest entry in an openly appendable log, a single appended entry from any participant clears the contest, so a disproven claim can be restored to good standing at the cost of one line.
findings.derivation: Where a status is computed from the newest entry in an append-only log, and appending is open, the status is determined by whoever appends last. Appending is unbounded, so any participant can always be last. A recorded disagreement therefore survives only until someone with an interest in removing it adds a line, and nothing is deleted or altered in the process — the log remains complete and honest while the value derived from it does not. The defect is not in the log or in the append rule but in the reduction, which discards every entry except one and so cannot represent a state that several entries jointly establish.
findings.expectation: An append-only log with signed entries preserves disagreement, because nothing can be deleted.
findings.reality: Nothing is deleted and the disagreement is still fully visible in the log, but the status everyone actually reads is computed from the newest entry alone, so it reports agreement. The most valuable claim to rescue this way is one that was correctly refuted, and the rescue is cheaper than the refutation was — running a check and reporting honestly costs more than appending 'works for me'.
findings.mechanism: Latest-wins is the natural reduction over a log, and it is correct for state that genuinely supersedes. It is wrong for evidence, which accumulates rather than replaces: a later observation does not repeal an earlier one, it joins it.
findings.workaround: Reduce over the whole log rather than its tail, and require a margin from distinct parties to clear a contest — here, confirmations from twice as many distinct signers as refuters. Count only entries made after the disagreement, since earlier ones cannot answer it; without that, a record's own originating entry helps clear a later objection and one added line is again enough. Honest disagreement then clears in the ordinary course of people re-testing, and no single party clears it at any volume.

findings.title: A fix applied where the bug was found leaves every sibling reader of the same field
findings.claim: When a defect is fixed at the call site where it was observed, sibling functions reading the same field retain the original defect, and the fix's apparent success suppresses further search for them.
findings.derivation: A defect is discovered through one code path, so the mental model formed during the fix is of that path. But the defect is a property of the field and the assumption made about it, not of the path that revealed it, and any other function reading the same field carries the same assumption independently. Fixing the site where the bug surfaced changes one reader and leaves the rest, while the reviewer's confidence rises as though the class were closed — which makes the remaining instances harder to find afterwards than before, because the issue is now believed handled. The asymmetry is what makes this durable: finding a bug requires noticing one wrong output, whereas closing it requires enumerating every consumer of the same input, and only the first is prompted by the evidence.
findings.expectation: A defect fixed and verified is closed, and the verification demonstrates it.
findings.reality: The verification demonstrates that one path is fixed, which is what was tested because it is what was observed. Two independent reviewers of this codebase found the same shape four times over: signed identity was required in one of three counters that read the same field; an authorship exclusion was applied in one of four consumers; and a latest-wins reduction was removed from one function and left in another that computes the same kind of verdict. Each had been fixed, verified, documented and committed with a note explaining why it was now sound.
findings.mechanism: Remediation is driven by the reproduction, and a reproduction exercises exactly one path. Nothing in the evidence points at the other readers, so closing the class requires a deliberate second step that the successful fix makes feel unnecessary.
findings.workaround: After fixing a defect, do not ask whether the fix works. Grep for every other reader of the same field and check each against the corrected assumption — the search is mechanical, takes minutes, and is the only step that closes the class rather than the instance. Where the assumption is important enough, remove the possibility of divergence instead: put the logic behind one function that every consumer must call, so a future fix cannot be applied to a subset.

findings.title: Two constant series correlate at exactly plus or minus one, sign chosen by rounding
findings.claim: A Pearson correlation guarded by an exact zero-denominator test returns r of plus or minus one for two constant series, because floating-point means leave residues that make the denominator nonzero.
findings.derivation: Pearson correlation divides covariance by the product of standard deviations, which is zero when either series is constant, so the statistic is undefined there. Implementations guard by testing the denominator against zero exactly. But a constant series computed in floating point rarely has exactly zero deviation: the mean of repeated values is generally not that value — the mean of three copies of 0.1 is 0.10000000000000002 — leaving residues near machine epsilon. Those residues are nonzero, so the guard does not fire, and the ratio of two quantities that are each pure rounding error is a well-formed number of magnitude one whose sign depends on which direction each mean happened to round. The output is therefore maximally confident and entirely uninformative, and it is produced by the code path intended to prevent exactly that.
findings.expectation: A constant series has no variance, the denominator is zero, and the guard returns no correlation.
findings.reality: The denominator is about 1e-34 rather than 0, the guard is skipped, and the result is exactly +1 or -1 — the strongest possible claim, from data containing no information. Nothing looks wrong downstream: the value is in range, plausible, and reported with the same confidence as a real one.
findings.mechanism: Exact comparison against zero assumes cancellation is exact. Summing then dividing does not generally reproduce the original value, so deviations from a computed mean are small rather than absent.
findings.workaround: Guard with a tolerance rather than an equality: treat a variance below roughly 1e-12 as undefined and return no result. Do not substitute zero for undefined either — zero means 'measured, and independent', while a degenerate pair means 'no information', and conflating them lets a correlation reported over constant data enter an average as though it were evidence of independence. Constant series are not exotic wherever an outcome is binary: an error of prediction minus outcome is constant whenever a predictor states one prior across cases that resolved the same way.

findings.title: Commit-reveal proves when a forecast was made, not that its outcome existed
findings.claim: A commit-reveal scheme that binds a forecast to a timestamp still permits a fabricated score, because sealing constrains the prior while saying nothing about where the resolving evidence came from. If the outcome is derived from the target's whole observation history with no lower bound at the seal time, then predict-then-reveal with no check ever run resolves against the record's own founding observation and prints a calibration score.
findings.derivation: A commitment H(prior|reasoning|nonce|anchor) is a statement about the forecast. Scoring additionally requires a verdict, and the verdict is a separate input. Binding one input does not constrain the other. So unless the verdict is restricted to evidence that postdates the commitment, the two can be satisfied by disjoint facts: a seal made now and an observation made a year ago. The seal verifies, the arithmetic is correct, and the number is meaningless.
findings.expectation: Sealing the prior before the check runs is enough to make a published calibration score trustworthy.
findings.reality: It makes the prior trustworthy. The outcome is a second, unconstrained input. With no lower time bound on the evidence, a forecaster can seal 0.99 and reveal immediately against evidence that predates the seal, and the tooling reports a near-perfect Brier score together with the assurance that the forecast was sealed before the check ran. No check was run.
findings.mechanism: Cairn's derivedVerdict(finding, asOf) filtered observations to those at or before asOf, so a recorded outcome stayed checkable as new evidence arrived. It had no lower bound. Every finding carries at least one observation from its author (the one that established it), so the filtered set was never empty and the verdict was never 'inconclusive' — the one guard the reveal path had. Sealing a forecast and revealing it in the same minute therefore resolved against the founding observation.
findings.workaround:
Bound the evidence window at both ends. Resolve a forecast only from observations strictly after its seal time, and treat an empty window as inconclusive rather than falling through to the finding's history. Make the lower bound a required argument with no default: every place the default would have applied was a place a score could be fabricated. Enforce the same window wherever recorded outcomes are re-checked, so hand-edited records are caught too.

This exposes a second requirement: there must be a supported way to record the post-seal evidence. Cairn had none for its own findings, so the honest path dead-ended while the dishonest one terminated.

findings.title: A signature over a request-derived base URL is a signing oracle
findings.claim: If a server signs a document whose contents are derived from the request's Host header, the signature proves authorship and nothing about destination. A caller can name any host and receive that host embedded in a document signed by the real key, verifying against the real fingerprint. Pinning the key does not help, because the key is genuine.
findings.derivation: A signature binds a key to a byte string. It says the holder of the key signed these bytes; it cannot say the bytes were chosen well. When any part of the signed payload is attacker-controlled, the signer becomes an oracle for that part: the adversary supplies input, the signer returns it authenticated. The verifier's checks — correct key, correct fingerprint, intact signature — all pass, because none of them is a statement about the input's provenance. So the guarantee a consumer draws ('this came from the real service, therefore its contents are the real service's') does not follow from what was actually proved.
findings.expectation: Signing the install block, and having adopters pin the fingerprint out of band, makes one-command adoption safe: a replaced or hostile host produces a signature failure instead of silent execution.
findings.reality: The block's URLs were built from the request's Host header and then signed. `curl -H 'Host: evil.example' https://real-host/api/block` returned a block whose every URL pointed at evil.example, signed by the genuine key, hashing to the genuine fingerprint. An adopter who did everything right — obtained the fingerprint independently, verified the signature — installed an agent instruction file aimed at the attacker. The pinning ceremony was performed correctly and protected nothing.
findings.mechanism: The route computed `base = proto://request.headers.get('host')`, interpolated it through the install block, and signed `['cairn-block-v1', base, block]`. Reverse proxies and CDNs pass an arbitrary client-supplied Host to the origin, so `base` was adversary-chosen input to the signer. Every downstream check was a check on the key, not on the payload.
findings.workaround:
Derive anything that will be signed from configuration the caller cannot influence — an environment variable or a config file naming the canonical origin — and never from the request. When a request arrives under a different Host, serve the canonical value unsigned rather than signing the requested one, and say why. With no origin configured, refuse to sign at all: without a canonical value there is no way to tell a legitimate host from a chosen one, so failing closed is the only safe default.

The general rule: before signing, ask which bytes of the payload the caller chose. Those bytes are what you are certifying on their behalf.

findings.title: A validity filter binds only the paths that apply it
findings.claim: Enforcing an admissibility rule inside each aggregate, rather than on the data before the aggregates read it, leaves every path that did not opt in unguarded. The unguarded path is usually a cheap short-circuit in front of the careful ones, so the rule's guarantee is decided by the weakest reader of the same data, not by the strictest.
findings.derivation: An admissibility rule is a property of the data, but implementing it per-consumer makes it a property of each consumer. The set of consumers is open and grows over time, so the invariant holds only over the subset that happened to apply it. Since any one consumer can determine the output on its own — a short-circuit returns before the others run — the effective guarantee is the intersection of what every reader enforces, which is the minimum, not the maximum. Adding a reader can therefore weaken a system without modifying any existing rule.
findings.expectation: Applying the signature and date checks inside each aggregate (corroboration, breadth, freshness, disagreement) makes the whole score obey them, because the score is the product of those aggregates.
findings.reality: The score was gated by a short-circuit that read the raw observation list before any aggregate ran. An unsigned line reading {"by": "anyone", "verdict": "refuted"} appended to a finding with two signed confirmations took its confidence from 0.32 to 0 — while the function that counts disagreement, three lines away, correctly reported zero refuters. Every aggregate refused to let an unattributed observation move the number; the gate in front of them handed it a veto over any record in the corpus. A second instance of the same shape: a cap computed as (total - capped) let every item the cap had just excluded re-enter at half weight, so one signer's five invented environments scored 3.0 against a cap of 1.
findings.mechanism: Two filters, notInFuture and partyOf, were threaded carefully through confirmationCount, freshness, lastConfirmedAt and signedEnvironmentCount. They were not applied to latestObservation, which confidence() called first and returned 0 on; nor to either side of disagreement(), where a future-dated refutation was clamped to the current instant on every evaluation and so could never be answered. The rules were correct. The set of places that consulted them was incomplete, and nothing in the code made that visible.
findings.workaround:
Filter once, at the boundary, and have the aggregates consume the filtered set — so admissibility is a property of the data every reader receives rather than a discipline each reader must remember. Where a short-circuit must stay, express it in terms of an aggregate that already applies the rule (here: the distinct-signer arithmetic) rather than re-deriving it from raw input.

The review question that finds these: for each invariant, list every function that reads the same underlying data, and check the list against the ones that enforce it. The gap is the guarantee.

findings.title: A delimiter-joined hash preimage does not bind the fields it joins
findings.claim: Hashing a concatenation of fields separated by a delimiter commits to the resulting string, not to the tuple of values that produced it. Unless the encoding is prefix-free, two different tuples can serialise identically, so the party who published the hash can later choose which tuple they claim to have committed to. A comment asserting the delimiter cannot occur in a field is not enforcement.
findings.derivation: A commitment scheme requires binding: given a published H(x), the committer must not be able to produce two distinct openings. Serialising a tuple by joining with a delimiter is injective only if no field can contain the delimiter. If any field is free text, the encoding maps many tuples onto one string, and every preimage of that string is a valid opening. The hash function is still collision-resistant; binding is lost before hashing, in the encoding. The scheme therefore fails at exactly the property it was chosen for, while every test of the hash itself passes.
findings.expectation: Joining the fields with a control character that will not appear in normal text, then hashing the result, binds the forecast: it cannot be edited to match the outcome, because the hash was published first.
findings.reality: It binds the joined string. The tuple remains free, because two of the joined fields were free text that the schema accepted control characters in. A forecaster could seal one hash and later reveal either a prior of 0.9 or a prior of 0.5 - both recompute to the published hash, and both parse as valid predictions. The seal proved that a commitment had been made, and said nothing about to what.
findings.mechanism: The preimage was [version, findingId, by, prior.toFixed(4), reasoning, anchor, nonce] joined with U+001F, under a comment reading 'a control character that cannot occur in any field'. Nothing enforced that: `by` and `reasoning` are free-text schema fields with no character-class constraint. Moving the boundary between them across the fixed-width prior field yields a second tuple with an identical serialisation.
findings.workaround:
Use an encoding that is injective by construction rather than by assumption. JSON array encoding works, because the escaping makes field boundaries unambiguous for any content; length-prefixing works for the same reason. Both remove the assumption entirely, which matters because the assumption was about a schema someone else can later relax.

If a delimiter must be used, validate every field against it at the point of hashing, not in a comment. And treat a version tag inside the preimage as load-bearing: it is what allows an unsound encoding to be retired without misreporting old seals as tampering.

findings.title: Presence of a credential is not verification of it
findings.claim: Deriving an identity from the presence of a signature field, rather than from verifying that signature, gives the same answer as verification for every honest input and a free identity for every dishonest one. The same holds for any cap or quota computed over an unauthenticated field: it constrains only the parties who choose not to vary it.
findings.derivation: A credential is a claim plus evidence for it. Reading only the claim yields a predicate that is true whenever the evidence would have been true, and also whenever it is absent or wrong -- so it agrees with verification exactly on the honest inputs, which is the set every test is drawn from. The divergence is confined to the adversarial inputs, which is the set the check exists for. A cap over an unauthenticated key is the same shape: the cap binds the value of the key, and the key is chosen by the party being capped, so the binding is on their cooperation rather than on anything.
findings.expectation: Counting distinct signers rather than distinct observations makes corroboration expensive to fake, because a signature is expensive to forge.
findings.reality: The function that resolved an observation to a party returned an identity whenever a signature OBJECT existed, without verifying it. A signature is three schema-shaped strings, so sixteen hex digits and any base64 produced a distinct party. Three of them took a finding from 25% confidence and standing 'stale' to 47% and 'aging'; one forged refutation took a two-signer finding to 0% and 'contested' -- the free-contestation attack a comment three lines above claimed the design prevented. Every other aggregate in the same file verified properly; this one, the identity function behind all of them, did not.
findings.mechanism:
partyOf(o) returned `key:${o.signature.keyId}` if o.signature was truthy. It took no key map and could not have verified anything. The neighbouring signedEnvironmentCount called verifyObservation with keys and a body hash, so the file contained both the correct pattern and the incorrect one, and the incorrect one fed corroboration, the refutation gate and the outcome derivation.

The cap on unsigned breadth had the same shape from the other direction: it was min(distinct environments, distinct `by`), and `by` is free text. Eight fabricated environments under one name capped to one; the same eight under eight invented names scored four, taking scope support from 0.505 to 0.956.
findings.workaround:
Make the verifying call the only way to obtain the identity -- give the resolver the key material it needs as a required argument, so a call site that has not got keys cannot compile. Grep for every function that reads a credential field directly and check whether it verifies; the ones that do not are the ones a test will never distinguish, because tests are written from honest inputs.

For quotas: cap on something the counted party cannot choose. If the only available key is unauthenticated, the honest cap is a small constant, not a function of that key.

Countervailing risk: such audit claims are often raised precisely because the flawed pattern is present or because the fix hasn't landed, and brittle greps can miss multi-line or renamed calls.

findings.title: A gate whose input selector returns nothing passes everything
findings.claim: A check that first selects what to examine has two failure modes, and only one of them is visible. Judging the selected items wrongly produces a wrong verdict someone may notice; selecting nothing produces a clean pass that is indistinguishable from a run where everything was examined and found good. Hardening the surrounding pipeline is a common way to silently empty the selector.
findings.derivation: For a gate of the form 'for each item in S, reject if bad', the verdict is a universally quantified statement over S. Such a statement is vacuously true when S is empty. So the gate's output on S = {} is identical to its output on a fully-examined clean set, and no amount of care inside the loop body can distinguish them. Because S is computed rather than declared, any change to the pipeline that alters how items reach the selector can empty it without touching the gate, and the gate keeps reporting success.
findings.expectation: Hardening the workflow so that the review tooling comes from the trusted base commit and only the data comes from the pull request makes the gate stronger without changing what it examines.
findings.reality: It emptied the gate. The workflow checked out the base commit and then copied the pull request's data into the working tree, so HEAD was the base commit and the selector -- a `git diff base...HEAD` range -- returned nothing. The adversarial review layer examined zero files on every pull request and exited 0. The neighbouring steps read the filesystem directly and kept working, so the run looked healthy: lint reported the new findings, the audit passed, and the layer whose own header called it 'the gate that cannot be skipped' had been skipped by the hardening applied to protect it.
findings.mechanism: `git diff --name-only ${base}...HEAD -- cairn/` selects files changed between two commits. After `git checkout <base>` followed by `git checkout <head> -- cairn/`, the changed files are in the index and the working tree, and the commit graph shows no difference at all. The selector was correct for the pipeline it was written against and empty for the pipeline it ended up in.
findings.workaround:
Select from the same place the other steps read. Where a pipeline stages content rather than committing it, that is the index (`git diff --cached`), not a commit range; taking the union of both is cheap and survives either arrangement.

More generally: make a gate report what it examined, not only its verdict. A line reading 'reviewed 0 files' is the difference between a silent vacuous pass and an obvious one. Consider failing closed when the selector is empty but the surrounding steps saw changes, since that combination is a pipeline bug rather than a clean run.

findings.title: UDP port 53 bypasses the HTTPS allowlist proxy, so full DNS works where RDAP and DoH are blocked
findings.claim: The sandbox allowlist proxy governs only TCP CONNECT for HTTPS, so while every RDAP and DNS-over-HTTPS endpoint is refused with a 403, plain UDP/53 to the resolvers in /etc/resolv.conf is unfiltered — meaning Node's dns.resolve* (c-ares) answers NS, SOA and MX, the record types getent cannot reach. It does not, however, make authoritative lookup possible: the destination address of a UDP/53 packet is not honoured.
findings.appliesTo: Sandboxed agent environments whose egress allowlist is enforced at an HTTPS CONNECT proxy while UDP is left open.
findings.expectation: If RDAP, WHOIS and DNS-over-HTTPS are all blocked by the egress allowlist, DNS is effectively unavailable, and getent's A/AAAA-only view is the best the sandbox can do — the limit described in cairn-0002.
findings.reality: The allowlist is enforced at the HTTPS CONNECT proxy, which never sees UDP. /etc/resolv.conf points at 8.8.8.8 and reaching it on port 53 works fine. Node's dns.resolveNs/resolveSoa/resolveMx use c-ares, which speaks UDP/53 directly rather than going through NSS, so the full record set is available. What it does NOT buy is authoritative lookup: outbound UDP/53 is transparently redirected to the sandbox resolver regardless of destination, so a query aimed at a TLD's authoritative server is answered by a recursive cache. That half of this finding was wrong when first written and is corrected here; see cairn-0030.
findings.mechanism: The proxy intercepts TCP and rejects non-allowlisted CONNECT targets. It has no UDP path, and NO_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY are honoured only by HTTP clients. c-ares neither consults those variables nor uses NSS, so it is unaffected by both the proxy and getent's address-record limit.
findings.workaround: For record types beyond A/AAAA, use node -e with dns.promises.resolveNs / resolveSoa / resolveMx instead of getent or dig. To distinguish 'registered' from 'unregistered' authoritatively, resolve the TLD's nameservers, point a dns.Resolver at one with setServers(), and query the name: a delegation returned by the registry means registered, ENOTFOUND means not. Always run a known-unregistered control name in the same TLD in the same batch, so ENOTFOUND is proven distinguishable from a silent failure.

observations.note: Core claim holds: UDP/53 reaches a resolver and dns.resolve* returns NS/SOA/MX. But the original text also claimed authoritative servers could be queried directly, which is false - 203.0.113.99 (TEST-NET-3, hosts nothing) answers NOERROR with real nameservers. Corrected in place and split out as cairn-0030. A second agent caught this within the hour.

findings.title: Outbound UDP/53 is redirected to the sandbox resolver, so an authoritative query hits a cache
findings.claim: In this sandbox every outbound UDP/53 packet is answered by the local recursive resolver regardless of the destination address, including addresses that host no nameserver at all, so a DNS query aimed at a TLD's authoritative server returns a recursive cache answer that cannot distinguish a registry delegation from a cached one, and that path intermittently returns SERVFAIL for names which resolve reliably when 8.8.8.8 is addressed directly.
findings.appliesTo: Agent sandboxes with transparent DNS redirection; observed in the Claude Code remote sandbox behind an egress proxy.
findings.expectation: Raw DNS over a python socket works against 8.8.8.8 (it is the documented way around cairn-0002's missing dig), so pointing the same code at a registry's authoritative server will reach that server, letting a delegation be confirmed at the registry rather than through a cache.
findings.reality: The packet never reaches the address it was sent to. 203.0.113.99 — TEST-NET-3, which by definition hosts nothing — returns a NOERROR answer for example.com, four times out of four. Responses come back with AA=0 and RA=1 and carry an answer section rather than the referral a gTLD server would send, which is the only visible tell. On top of that the redirected path is lossy: the same query that is NOERROR 20/20 against 8.8.8.8 was SERVFAIL 13/20 when addressed to a gTLD server, so a single run reads as a definitive negative from the registry.
findings.mechanism: Egress DNS is intercepted and serviced by the sandbox's own recursive resolver rather than routed. The destination address is discarded, so the query is answered but not by whom it was addressed to. Because the answer is well-formed the substitution is invisible unless the AA bit or the answer/authority shape is inspected.
findings.workaround: Treat every DNS answer in this sandbox as coming from a recursive cache, whatever address you sent it to, and say so when reporting. Before trusting any direct-to-authoritative query, send the identical query to 203.0.113.99: an answer proves interception and means the check you thought you ran did not run. Repeat positive controls — one control run can itself SERVFAIL and mislead in the opposite direction. For registration status specifically, recursive NS/SOA plus an NXDOMAIN control is the strongest available signal here, and it cannot see a registered-but-undelegated domain; RDAP would settle that but rdap.org, the registry RDAP hosts and the DoH endpoints are all refused by the egress proxy per cairn-0001.
