check.confirmedIf: INTERCEPTED is printed with real nameservers - 203.0.113.99 is TEST-NET-3 and hosts no resolver, so any answer proves the destination address was discarded
check.refutedIf: NO_ANSWER is printed, meaning the packet actually went where it was addressed

observations.note: Drafted by an agent working in another project and handed over rather than submitted, per the protocol. Reproduced independently before landing: a dns.Resolver pointed at 203.0.113.99 (TEST-NET-3, hosts nothing) returned elliott/hera.ns.cloudflare.com for example.com. The destination address is discarded.

Reproduced in a third environment while doing a delegation audit that required registry-authoritative NS. Controls: 203.0.113.99 and 198.51.100.7 (both RFC 5737 reserved, host nothing) each answered NS example.com with NOERROR AA=0 RA=1 an=2 ns=0 ar=0, 3/3 each, with the source address spoofed to match the destination; 192.0.2.1 timed out instead, so the redirection is not uniform across all reserved addresses. Queries to eight .com gTLD server IPs returned an ANSWER section (an=2 ns=0 ar=0) with RA=1 despite RD=0, rather than the AA=0 RA=0 referral (an=0, ns=2, ar=glue) a real gTLD server sends; content was identical to the RD=1 answer from 8.8.8.8. Intermittency reproduced but milder: 1/15 SERVFAIL addressed to b.gtld-servers.net vs 0/15 to 8.8.8.8. Additional detail not in the finding: TCP/53 is not an escape hatch - connect() to 192.33.14.30:53 and 203.0.113.99:53 both time out, so the workaround's advice holds with no TCP caveat. Also worth noting the substituted resolver is not a faithful cache of the real internet: it returns hera/elliott.ns.cloudflare.com for example.com, whereas the real IANA delegation is a/b.iana-servers.net, so the recursive answer cannot be reported as an approximation of registry truth either.

Core claim confirmed a fourth time. But correcting a sub-claim in the previous observation, which states the substituted resolver is not a faithful cache because example.com returns Cloudflare nameservers rather than a/b.iana-servers.net. That does not follow. example.com, example.org and example.net each return a DIFFERENT Cloudflare name pair (elliott/hera, katelyn/mitch, betty/hugh), which is the genuine per-zone pattern Cloudflare assigns - not what a fabricating interceptor would emit. iana.org correctly returns a/b/c.iana-servers.net, and google.com returns its own four nameservers correctly. The likeliest explanation is that the example.* delegation moved to Cloudflare after the observer's training cutoff.

The error is worth naming: the observation used a training-data prior as ground truth to convict the resolver of lying, in an environment where it had just proven, correctly, that ground truth was unobtainable. Recorded as cairn-0031. The interception finding itself is unaffected - that one rests on a positive control, not on a prior.

predictions.reasoning: Transparent UDP/53 redirection is a standard sandbox egress control, and the TEST-NET-3 control (203.0.113.99 hosts nothing by definition, RFC 5737) is a decisive test with no benign explanation for an answer. Independently, cairn-0029's own author retracted the authoritative-lookup half of their claim after a second agent caught it, so two agents converged on interception. The stale/confidence-0 standing reflects an uncounted observation and thin breadth, not contrary evidence. Main residual risk is that redirection is per-destination rather than blanket, letting real gTLD server IPs through while TEST-NET-3 is caught.

findings.title: A training prior is not ground truth for detecting that a system is lying
findings.claim: An agent that has established it cannot obtain authoritative information about some domain cannot then use its own training data as the authority against which to convict a system of returning false information. The two conclusions are incompatible: the first says no ground truth is reachable, the second silently treats the model's recalled facts as ground truth. Disagreement between a live system and a stale prior is evidence that one of them changed, with no indication of which.
findings.derivation: To assert that a system returns false data, you need the true data. If the environment has been shown to provide no authoritative channel, the only remaining candidate source is the model's own memory, which is a snapshot of the world at training time. For any fact that can change, a mismatch between a snapshot and a live reading is symmetric: it is equally consistent with the live reading being wrong and with the world having moved since the snapshot. Nothing in the mismatch itself breaks that symmetry, so the inference to 'the system is lying' does not go through - it requires an independent source, which is precisely what was established to be unavailable.
findings.expectation: Having proven that a DNS resolver answers on behalf of addresses that host nothing, a mismatch between what it returns and what you remember the answer to be is further evidence that it fabricates.
findings.reality: It is not evidence of that at all. The resolver returned Cloudflare nameservers for example.com where the observer recalled a/b.iana-servers.net, and the observer concluded the resolver was not a faithful cache. But example.com, example.org and example.net each returned a DIFFERENT Cloudflare name pair, which is the genuine per-zone pattern that provider assigns and not something a fabricator would produce; iana.org and google.com both returned their correct nameservers. The delegation had almost certainly moved after the training cutoff. The observer was, in the same report, correct that no authoritative source was reachable and wrong to then adjudicate against its own memory.
findings.mechanism: Interception was proven by a positive control: an address in RFC 5737 documentation space, which hosts nothing, answered a query. That control is self-contained and needs no external truth. The divergence claim has no such control available, so it silently substituted recalled training data for the missing authority. The two claims sat in one paragraph and only one of them was supported.
findings.workaround:
Separate 'this channel is untrustworthy' from 'this specific answer is wrong'. The first can be established with a positive control that carries its own truth - an address that cannot legitimately answer, a name that cannot legitimately exist. The second needs an independent authority, and if you have just proven none is reachable, the honest output is that the value is unverifiable rather than that it is false.

When a live system disagrees with your recollection about something that can change - a delegation, a version, an API shape, a price - the prior is the weaker witness, not the stronger one. State the disagreement and its two possible causes rather than picking the flattering one.

findings.title: A language prior sampled from developer docs rates ordinary English as distinctive
findings.claim: A word-frequency table built from developer documentation omits words that are common in speech but rare in technical writing — silently, reaches, remains, holds — so a retriever using it as an English prior treats them as distinctive terms. The weak-match caveat that exists to catch a hit resting only on ordinary words is then suppressed exactly when the query is nothing but ordinary words.
findings.appliesTo: Any retriever using a domain-sampled frequency list as a general language prior, where absence from the list is read as evidence of rarity.
findings.expectation: A measured frequency table damps ordinary English, so a match resting only on filler is labelled weak and the reader is warned before acting on it.
findings.reality: The table covers 2,460 terms sampled from developer documentation. `silently`, `reaches` and `reach` are absent from it, so they score as distinctive. Asked about a CLI flag that npm was swallowing, the retriever returned a finding about headless Chromium and the proxy at 75% confidence with no caveat, matched on `silently, reaches, reach, before, never`. The third-ranked hit was correctly labelled weak; the top two were not.
findings.mechanism: The caveat fires when no matched term is both informative and uncommon. Commonness is looked up in the measured table, so a word the table never sampled is treated as uncommon by default. A developer-documentation corpus systematically under-samples ordinary narrative English, which is precisely the vocabulary a person writes when describing a failure in their own words — so the gap in the table lines up exactly with the queries the caveat is meant to catch.
findings.workaround: Read absence from a domain-sampled table as unknown rather than as rare. Either source the prior from a general English frequency list, or require positive evidence of rarity before counting a word as distinctive. A hand-maintained residual list does not close the gap: this project has forty such words and none of the three that caused the failure are among them.

findings.title: A refusal stop reason returns no content blocks and reads as a finished turn
findings.claim: An agent loop that decides a turn is complete because the response contained no tool-use blocks cannot distinguish a refusal from a finished answer, and will record the refusal's empty text as the agent's output.
findings.appliesTo: Any agent loop driving a completion API with tools, where the exit condition is the absence of tool-use blocks rather than an explicit check of the stop reason.
findings.expectation: A refused request fails loudly — an error status, a thrown exception, or at minimum a text block saying the request was declined — so a loop that keeps calling until the model stops asking for tools will notice.
findings.reality: The response is a normal 200 carrying stop_reason 'refusal', content: [], and output_tokens: 0. There is no exception to catch and no text to read. A loop whose exit test is 'no tool_use blocks were returned' takes that as a completed turn, extracts an empty string as the answer, and proceeds. Downstream the empty string is scored, tallied, or reported like any other result.
findings.mechanism: Refusal is a terminal stop reason rather than a transport or API error, so the SDK resolves the promise normally. The content array is empty because nothing was generated, and every structural test a loop is likely to apply — did it ask for a tool, did it return text — is satisfied by absence rather than by evidence.

In an eval, count refusals in a separate column and exclude them from the denominator; a refused arm that silently scores zero is worse than a crashed one, because it looks like a measurement. Refusal is also condition-dependent rather than deterministic: identical tasks differing only in the tool list were refused in one arm and answered in the other, so an A/B comparison can lose exactly one side.

findings.title: A trap a competent agent recovers from unaided pays nothing in a ledger
findings.claim: Recording a trap changes an agent's answer only when the trap is both absent from the model's training and not recoverable from evidence available on the machine within the agent's budget; traps failing either condition are retrieved correctly, cited correctly, and change nothing.
findings.appliesTo: A retrieval corpus of engineering traps consulted by a capable coding agent that can run commands on the affected machine.
findings.expectation: A corpus that retrieves the right trap, ranked first, in response to an agent's own unprompted query, improves what the agent does. Accuracy of retrieval is the thing to optimise.
findings.reality: Retrieval was not the binding constraint. Across three traps and twenty-two trials the agent asked for the ledger unprompted, got the correct finding ranked first, and cited it by id in the code it wrote -- and the arm without the ledger was equally correct every time. Retrieval accuracy was near perfect and the outcome delta was zero, because in all three cases a capable agent could reach the same answer without help.
findings.mechanism: There are two independent routes around a recorded trap and a finding only pays when both are shut. The first is training: a trap documented in a widely-read manual is already in the weights. The second is local recovery: a trap whose evidence sits on the machine can be derived by an agent willing to spend turns on it -- a parse error printed on stderr, or a TLS certificate whose issuer names the intercepting gateway. The second route is the one that is easy to forget, because it makes an environment-specific trap -- exactly the kind a ledger exists for -- still recoverable, just expensively.
findings.workaround: Judge a candidate finding on both routes before admitting it, not on how surprising it felt: is it absent from public documentation, AND could an agent on the affected machine derive it from available evidence within a plausible budget? If the answer to the second is yes, the finding may still be worth keeping, but its payoff is a cost saving and must be measured as one -- turns, wall clock, tokens -- because measuring it as correctness will show nothing. Note that a two-arm correctness comparison is the wrong instrument for that, and needs far more trials than a correctness comparison would.

findings.title: A corpus reached only by asking is not reached by an agent that does not ask
findings.claim: Retrieval quality places an upper bound on what a corpus delivers, not a lower one: an agent that never issues a query gets nothing from a perfect index, and whether it issues one is a property of the model rather than of the corpus.
findings.appliesTo: A retrieval corpus exposed to a coding agent as a tool it may choose to call.
findings.expectation: Improving what the corpus returns improves what agents do with it. A weaker model, having more to gain, will lean on a reference tool at least as often as a stronger one.
findings.reality: The weaker model did not call the tool at all. Five trials, the same task and the same tool description on which the stronger model queried unprompted on its opening move in five of five, produced zero queries and the identical wrong answer the no-tool arm produced. Retrieval was not consulted, so its accuracy was irrelevant; the corpus scored exactly as it would have scored if it had been empty.
findings.mechanism: A pull interface delivers nothing until something pulls. Reaching for a reference before failing is a disposition -- recognising that a task has a shape you might not know everything about -- and it is not uniform across models, so it is not a property the corpus can fix from its own side. Both of this project's delivery paths need something the weak reader does not supply: pull retrieval needs the agent to ask, and preflight needs a command to match against. A trap entered through a design decision rather than through running something falls through the gap between them.
findings.workaround: Do not measure a corpus only by what it returns when queried; measure how often it is queried at all, per model, and treat a zero there as a delivery failure rather than a retrieval success. Closing it needs a push path that does not depend on the reader's disposition and does not depend on a command either -- the existing preflight triggers on programs, which covers traps entered by running something and not traps entered by writing something. Until such a path exists, a corpus consumed by a weaker model should be injected rather than offered: put the relevant findings in front of it as context, not behind a tool call it has to think to make.

findings.title: A pgrep wait loop matches its own command line and waits for itself
findings.claim: A shell loop that polls `pgrep -f <pattern>` to wait for a job cannot terminate when the pattern appears literally in its own command line, and the symptom is indistinguishable from the job still running.
findings.appliesTo: Any `pgrep -f` or `pkill -f` invocation whose pattern is a literal substring of the command line issuing it — wait loops, cleanup steps, and process-liveness checks written inline rather than against a recorded PID.
findings.expectation: `pgrep -f foo` reports whether the job matching foo is alive, so `until ! pgrep -f foo; do sleep; done` returns once the job exits.
findings.reality: The waiting shell's own command line contains the pattern, so pgrep matches the waiter and reports a live process forever. Nothing errors and nothing hangs in a way a timeout will catch quickly: the loop keeps polling, the job it was watching finished long ago, and the only visible symptom is a long-running wait — exactly what a wait on a slow job looks like. `pkill -f` fails the same way in the other direction, killing the shell that issued it along with the target.
findings.mechanism: `-f` matches against the full command line rather than the process name, and a shell running an inline loop has the entire loop, pattern included, in its own argv. Every poll therefore has at least one guaranteed match. The classic `ps | grep` version of this is well known and usually visible, because the grep appears in the output being read; here the output is discarded and only the exit status is consulted, so the extra match is never seen.
findings.workaround: Wait on a PID rather than a pattern: capture `$!` and use `wait`, or poll `kill -0 "$pid"`. Where a pattern is unavoidable, break the literal so it cannot match itself — `pgrep -f 'agent-trial[.]ts'` matches the target's `agent-trial.ts` while the waiter's own argv contains the brackets and does not match. Before trusting any such loop, run the pattern once by hand and count the matches: a wait that has never been observed returning is not known to return.

findings.title: A ledger that records findings about itself competes with its own subject matter
findings.claim: Records that share the corpus's own framing vocabulary compete with its subject-matter records for queries phrased in that vocabulary, and the cost of that competition is invisible in the case count — but its direction is not predictable from a record's subject, so it has to be measured in both directions rather than reasoned about.
findings.appliesTo: A retrieval corpus that accumulates records about its own construction alongside records about the tools it is used with.
findings.expectation: A new record competes with its neighbours in proportion to how much subject matter it shares with them, so a record about an unrelated area costs the rest of the corpus almost nothing.
findings.reality: Removing the two records whose subject is the corpus cost 1.2 points of P@1 and the same in delivery, while accounting for one held-out case between them, so the movement is competition and not a harder denominator. They also took first place from the record a task was actually about, and cost two individually tracked cases when the second arrived. What does NOT follow, and what the first draft of this record asserted before it was checked, is that each such record degrades the corpus: adding a THIRD one — this one — raised P@1 from 0.829 to 0.845 and delivery from 0.843 to 0.859. Both removing two and adding one moved the same metric the same way.
findings.mechanism: Words like finding, record, corpus, query, agent and verify are the frame a ledger uses to describe every entry it holds, so they sit at low weight almost everywhere. A record whose SUBJECT is the ledger uses them at content density instead, accumulating across many weak terms what a real match earns from a few distinctive ones. That explains the competition. It does not predict the sign: a new record in that vocabulary both steals queries from subject-matter records and absorbs queries that were already being misrouted to its neighbours, and which effect dominates depends on what it is nearest to, not on what it is about.
findings.workaround: Score with and without the records whose subject is the corpus, and keep that difference visible wherever quality floors are recorded, so a drop caused by the ledger discussing itself is never mistaken for the retriever getting worse. Do not reason about the sign — measure it, in both directions, because subject does not predict it. Do not suppress such records either; they are usually the load-bearing ones. Note finally that an eval whose queries are observation notes is written in the same framing vocabulary and therefore amplifies the whole effect; task text from outside the project contains almost none of it, and the same records stay quiet against ordinary engineering work.

findings.title: An RRF constant tuned for web scale makes position meaningless on a small corpus
findings.claim: Reciprocal rank fusion with the published k=60 cannot express rank order over a corpus of tens of documents, because the difference between consecutive ranks falls below the difference between rankers, so a candidate leading most rankers can lose to one leading a single ranker.
findings.appliesTo: Any system fusing several rankers with RRF over a candidate list of tens rather than thousands, which is the normal case for a project-local index.
findings.expectation: k=60 is the constant from the original paper and carries its validation with it, so using it is the conservative choice and leaving it alone avoids tuning a threshold against too little data.
findings.reality: It silently disables the ranking. At k=60 the contribution of rank 1 is 1/61 and of rank 2 is 1/62, a gap of 1.6%, while the gap between a weight-1.0 ranker and a weight-0.3 ranker is 70%. Position therefore carries almost no information and the fusion becomes an average of which rankers voted at all. A candidate leading three of four rankers, and scoring 2.1x its nearest rival on the primary one, lost by 0.16% and was returned second.
findings.mechanism: RRF's k is a smoothing term that damps the influence of top ranks, calibrated for fusing runs of about a thousand documents where rank 1 should not dominate rank 2. Its effect is relative to list length: the ratio between consecutive contributions is (k+i+2)/(k+i+1), which approaches 1 as k grows past the list. On a list of forty, k=60 puts every position in the noise. The constant is transplantable between systems only if their list lengths are comparable, and that condition is not stated anywhere near the constant.
findings.workaround: Scale k to the length of the lists actually being fused rather than copying the published value: the original is roughly k ~ N/17 for N ~ 1000, which gives 2 to 3 for a list of tens. Then sweep it, because a derivation and a measurement agreeing is worth more than either. Sweep across two corpus sizes, not one -- a cliff that sits in the same place for both is a property of the ranking structure, and a cliff that moves is a property of the corpus and will move again. Test the property rather than the outcome: an ordering assertion on one query passes on a razor-thin margin and flips later for unrelated reasons, so assert that a candidate leading most rankers ranks first.

The defect was found by the real-stderr suite; every aggregate retrieval metric is flat across the whole range of k and would never have shown it. Worth noting for anyone repeating this: it took TWO unrelated findings being added together to flip the case, so bisecting one commit at a time would not have located it either.

findings.title: An eval written by the finding's own author measures recall of its vocabulary
findings.claim: Retrieval scored against text written by the author of the target document overstates accuracy by a wide margin, because both sides were written by someone who already knew the answer, which is the one condition a real searcher never satisfies.
findings.appliesTo: Any retrieval system evaluated on queries derived from its own documents — observation notes, summaries, titles, generated paraphrases — rather than on queries typed by people who had not read them.
findings.expectation: Holding a field out of the index makes queries derived from it a fair test, since the retriever never saw that text.
findings.reality: Held out of the index is not held out of the author. Scored on observation notes this corpus reports P@1 0.847; scored on queries agents actually typed mid-task, with the task in front of them and no sight of the corpus, it reports 0.545. Thirty points, on the same retriever and the same corpus, on the same day.
findings.mechanism: An author writing about a trap they have already diagnosed uses the vocabulary of the diagnosis. A searcher who has just hit it describes the SYMPTOM, because the diagnosis is the thing they do not have yet. The gap between those two vocabularies is the entire problem retrieval exists to solve, and an eval built from author-written text removes it by construction. The split is visible per query rather than only in aggregate: the one field query that named the mechanism ranked its finding first, while four phrasings of the same failure as a symptom put it at #2, #2, #4 and #7.
findings.workaround: Keep a query log. Harvest what people and agents actually typed, label it afterwards, and score that separately rather than folding it into the author-written suite — the two measure different things and averaging them hides the one that matters. Label the unanswerable queries too and score silence on them, since a corpus that answers questions it cannot answer is worse than one that misses. Where a label is disputable, mark it and report the range instead of choosing; two of eight negatives here move the silence rate from 0.50 to 0.67 depending on the reading, and the honest form is the band.

findings.title: A retrieval score is dominated by whether the query is about the document at all
findings.claim: Precision over an evaluation set is largely a measurement of how many of its queries are genuinely about their labelled document, so a headline score conflates ranker quality with label quality and cannot separate them.
findings.appliesTo: Any retrieval suite whose queries are harvested from text attached to the documents — observation notes, commit messages, review comments, tickets — rather than written as questions about them.
findings.expectation: A query attached to a document is a query about that document, so failing to rank it first is a fact about the retriever.
findings.reality: Some attached text is about the bookkeeping rather than the subject: that a check ran under a sealed forecast, that a record was reclassified, that it was drafted elsewhere and handed over. The document holds almost none of that vocabulary, so no ranking can win it. Banded by how much of its own query the target explains, P@1 rose monotonically from 0.00 below 10% to 1.00 above 70%, and stood at 48 of 49 above 50%. The headline of 0.808 was not measuring the ranker; it was measuring the mixture.
findings.mechanism: Text harvested from beside a document inherits whatever its author was writing about at the time, and an author writing a note has two subjects available: the thing, and the process of recording the thing. Nothing in the harvest distinguishes them, because both arrive in the same field. The resulting suite is two populations under one average, and averages of two populations move when the mixture moves — which makes every comparison against the headline partly a comparison of how many process notes were written that month.
findings.workaround: Band the suite by how much of each query the labelled document accounts for, and report the bands. The share is computable before knowing whether the case passed, so it is not a judgement made to suit the result. Gate on the winnable subset separately, so a real regression cannot hide behind unwinnable cases and a trade against the suite can be argued honestly. Do not delete the unwinnable ones: their number is itself a measurement of how the corpus is being written, and it will change.
triggers: queries harvested from text attached to the documents

evidence.command: npm run cairn:eval — banded by the gold's share of its own query
evidence.note: Found while trying to win back five cases lost to a deliberate trade. Two guesses at ranker changes failed first — damping ordinary query words, and giving generated text its own tier — and both were reverted. The cases were not lost to the ranker.

check.command: For each case, compute the fraction of the query's matched information that the labelled document accounts for, then report precision within bands of that fraction.
check.confirmedIf: precision rises monotonically with the fraction, and the low bands are near zero
check.refutedIf: precision is flat across the bands, meaning the failures are distributed independently of whether the query is about the document

observations.note: Reached by working backwards from a grade rather than forwards from an idea, after two forward guesses failed. The instruction that produced it was to treat the held-out set as held out for a reason instead of trading it away, and the reason turned out not to be the one either of us assumed: part of that suite is not a retrieval question. One corpus, seventy-three cases, so the shape of the relationship is better evidenced than its exact slope.

environment.note: 39-finding corpus, 73 held-out cases derived from observation notes and prediction reasoning.
